newsitem.title: CHINA: China steel industry needs major overhaul - analysts.
newsitem.headline: China steel industry needs major overhaul - analysts.

text.p: China's loss-making steel industry needs a major overhaul, including new investment and a big shift in product varieties if it is ever to move into profit, industry analysts said on Friday.
The big state-owned steel mills, long supported by the government, could no longer count on being bailed out and had to look to financing new equipment themselves, they said.
Small and medium-sized producers faced the threat of being merged or eventually being allowed to go bankrupt, the analysts said.

"The steel industry is making big losses, and it's hard to see a turn-around in the situation in the next few years," said an analyst with a Shanghai brokerage house. China has 2,000 steel factories, only 75 of which made a profit last year, mostly the bigger ones, analysts said. The main problem is the inability of most mills to produce the high-value steel varieties required by the market.

"China's steel products cannot cater for market demand," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage. "Low-quality, low-technology products which are hard to sell account for nearly half the total output."
China's steel market was sluggish in 1996 with demand growing only three percent compared to a huge jump of 27 percent in 1995, the China Securities newspaper reported recently.

Official figures show China's crude steel output topped 100 million tonnes in 1996, making it the biggest steel producer in the world. But analysts said the figures masked a serious supply-and-demand imbalance.

"On the one hand, low-value products are piling up in the warehouses, while on the other hand, China still needs to import many high-value steel types," said an analyst with one of the biggest domestic brokerages.

"For example, steel sections are in seriously oversupply, with 25 percent of production capacity idle at present," he said. "But cold rod sheets are in a shortage with nearly 30 percent of demand covered by imports."
China imported 16 million tonnes of steel in 1996, up from 13 million in 1995 after import tariffs for steel products were cut by an average of 30 percent in 1996, official figures showed.
"In order to compete with imported products, prices for most domestic products were cut last year," said a local analyst.
Of 29 steel products, prices for 24 products were cut by an average of four to eight percent, official figures showed.
Analysts said they did not expect a quick reverse of losses due to difficulties in raising funds for updating technology and adjusting varieties.
"It is not easy for steel mills to raise money from the stock market. The steel firms already listed are not performing well," said an analyst with a local brokerage.

The average earnings per share for the 14 steel shares listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses was only 0.06 yuan in the first half of 1996. The figure was 0.11 yuan in 1995 and 0.23 in 1994, the China Securites newspaper said.

"China's government may take action to support some big steel mills," said an analyst with a big foreign iron ore supplier in Shanghai. "But the support will be limited because the government may not have sufficient funds."
"As to small ones, their fate is unavoidably to be merged or to go bankrupt," the analyst said.
"Almost all steel makers in China face a shortage of working capital," he said. "Even the most profitable, Baoshan Steel, has borrowed 50 million yuan recently due to insufficient working capital."
